analysis.one_liner: Bans paying garment workers by piece rate and requires garment makers to register with the Labor Department.
analysis.headline: A bill protecting garment workers from below-minimum piece-rate pay was introduced in September 2026 and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal wage law to make it illegal for garment industry employers to pay workers by piece rate, meaning by each item sewn instead of by the hour. It would also require garment manufacturers and contractors to register with the Department of Labor, giving federal inspectors a clear list of who is in the industry. The purpose is to stop a pay practice that garment workers' advocates say lets factories pay some immigrant workers less than the minimum wage and shields fly-by-night contractors from accountability. The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026, less than four months before this Congress ends, and has been referred to committee with no further action. [S1][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers, who are heavily immigrant and often paid by the item sewn, would get guaranteed hourly protection instead of piece rates that can fall below the minimum wage once a factory's sewing lines are measured. Lawful, larger manufacturers also gain from competitors being forced to register and follow the same rules. [S1]

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit garment industry employers from paying employees by piece rate, replacing item-by-item pay with hourly pay that cannot fall below the federal floor. [S1]

The bill would require manufacturers and contractors in the garment industry to register with the Department of Labor, giving the agency a roster of who operates in the trade and a lever to pull when wage violations surface. [S1]

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and contractors, especially small shops that run on piece rates and thin margins, would bear the cost of restructured pay, registration, and possible Department of Labor enforcement. Some of that cost could show up in apparel prices or in shops leaving the business. [S1]

drawbacks.text: A piece-rate ban removes pay flexibility that some fast, experienced sewers have preferred, and shifts factories toward hourly structures that increase labor costs; small contractors operating on thin margins could consolidate or exit rather than comply. This is the standard cost of extending stronger wage protection to a low-margin industry. [S1]

Registration with the Department of Labor adds paperwork and a compliance hurdle for small shops, and the bill's practical value depends entirely on enforcement resources that the text alone does not guarantee. [S1]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For garment workers, the bill addresses a real and documented pattern: piece rates in this trade can leave sewers earning below the minimum wage for their hours, and registration targets the contractor chains that let violations hide behind layers of subcontracting. The cost falls on employers in a low-margin industry, and some may pass costs to consumers or cut jobs rather than comply. On balance the protections are aimed at a specific, measurable wage problem, but the bill has attracted only narrow support and no committee action, so it delivers nothing yet.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it with the Congress set to end in early January 2027. [S3]

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill in the House on September 14, 2026. [S1][S3]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, the committee with jurisdiction over federal wage law. [S3]
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all from one party, and no Republicans signed on. [S2]
Since referral, the bill's only listed action is that referral; there is no committee vote, hearing, or floor action in its history. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no action taken yet, no one has won or lost. If the bill dies in committee, garment employers who pay by piece rate are the clear beneficiaries, because the pay and registration requirements would never take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; piece-rate employers if it dies

for.name: Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban piece-rate pay in the garment industry and require industry registration with the Department of Labor. [S1]

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; no votes have occurred to show how the parties would split. [S2]

industries.note: The bill bans the piece-rate pay structures many of these shops rely on and adds a registration requirement, raising labor costs in a low-margin industry. Its interest runs against workers here: piece-rate pay is the mechanism by which some shops pay sewers less than the minimum wage for their hours. [S1]
Employers that already pay hourly wages gain from rivals being required to register and follow the same pay rules, leveling competition against contractors who cut corners. [S1]

analysis.trajectory: Introduced with the Congress ending in early January 2027, referred to a committee with no hearing, markup, or floor action on record, and holding only eight cosponsors from one party, the bill is very likely to die in committee when the Congress adjourns; its practical path would be reintroduction in the next Congress. [S2][S3]
